```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}

# Bd data plot used by several figures
plot_bd <- function(...) {
  plot(r ~ temp, data = bd, pch = 16, col = "grey45", xlab = "Temperature (°C)",
       ylab = "Growth rate r (per day)", ...)
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey85")
}

# Layered DAG: one horizontal band per level of the hierarchy
# nodes: list of list(id, lab (expression or string), x, y, type)
#   type: "latent" (open circle), "data" (shaded circle),
#         "fixed" (square: prior constant), "covariate" (shaded square); lty = 2 dashes a box
# edges: character matrix (from, to, optional bend for a curved arrow)
# levels: data.frame(lab, ymin, ymax); plates: list of list(x0, x1, y0, y1, lab)
draw_level_dag <- function(nodes, edges, levels, plates = list(), xlim, main = "",
                           r = 0.36, cex = 1, level_x = xlim[1] + 0.05) {
  par(mar = c(0.2, 0.2, if (nzchar(main)) 1.6 else 0.2, 0.2))
  ylim <- range(c(levels$ymin, levels$ymax))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  if (nzchar(main)) mtext(main, side = 3, line = 0.3, font = 2, cex = cex)
  band_cols <- rep(c("grey96", "white"), length.out = nrow(levels))
  usr <- par("usr")
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(levels))) {
    rect(usr[1], levels$ymin[k], usr[2], levels$ymax[k], col = band_cols[k], border = NA)
    text(level_x, levels$ymax[k] - 0.12, levels$lab[k], adj = c(0, 1), cex = cex * 0.75,
         font = 3, col = "grey30")
  }
  abline(h = unique(c(levels$ymin, levels$ymax))[-c(1)], col = "grey80", lty = 3)
  for (p in plates) {
    rect(p$x0, p$y0, p$x1, p$y1, border = "grey35", lwd = 1.2)
    if (isTRUE(p$left)) {
      text(p$x0 + 0.08, p$y0 + 0.06, p$lab, adj = c(0, 0), cex = cex * 0.72, col = "grey25")
    } else if (isTRUE(p$top)) {
      text(p$x1 - 0.08, p$y1 - 0.08, p$lab, adj = c(1, 1), cex = cex * 0.72, col = "grey25")
    } else {
      text(p$x1 - 0.08, p$y0 + 0.08, p$lab, adj = c(1, 0), cex = cex * 0.72, col = "grey25")
    }
  }
  ids <- vapply(nodes, `[[`, "", "id")
  half <- function(n) {
    w <- if (is.null(n$w)) max(r, 0.5 * strwidth(n$lab, cex = cex) + 0.1) else n$w
    c(w, r * 0.8)
  }
  edge_point <- function(n, dx, dy) {
    if (n$type %in% c("latent", "data")) {
      s <- if (is.null(n$w)) 1 else n$w / r
      d <- sqrt((dx / s)^2 + dy^2)
      return(c(n$x, n$y) + r * c(dx, dy) / d)
    }
    h <- half(n)
    t <- min(h[1] / abs(dx), h[2] / abs(dy))
    c(n$x, n$y) + t * c(dx, dy)
  }
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(edges))) {
    a <- nodes[[match(edges[k, 1], ids)]]
    b <- nodes[[match(edges[k, 2], ids)]]
    bend <- if (ncol(edges) > 2 && !is.na(edges[k, 3])) as.numeric(edges[k, 3]) else 0
    if (bend == 0) {
      dx <- b$x - a$x
      dy <- b$y - a$y
      p0 <- edge_point(a, dx, dy)
      p1 <- edge_point(b, -dx, -dy)
      arrows(p0[1], p0[2], p1[1], p1[2], length = 0.07, lwd = 1.3, col = "grey20")
    } else {
      # quadratic curve bowed by `bend` (perpendicular, to the left of a -> b)
      len <- sqrt((b$x - a$x)^2 + (b$y - a$y)^2)
      cx <- (a$x + b$x) / 2 - bend * (b$y - a$y) / len
      cy <- (a$y + b$y) / 2 + bend * (b$x - a$x) / len
      p0 <- edge_point(a, cx - a$x, cy - a$y)
      p1 <- edge_point(b, cx - b$x, cy - b$y)
      tt <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 40)
      qx <- (1 - tt)^2 * p0[1] + 2 * tt * (1 - tt) * cx + tt^2 * p1[1]
      qy <- (1 - tt)^2 * p0[2] + 2 * tt * (1 - tt) * cy + tt^2 * p1[2]
      lines(qx[-40], qy[-40], lwd = 1.3, col = "grey20")
      arrows(qx[39], qy[39], qx[40], qy[40], length = 0.07, lwd = 1.3, col = "grey20")
    }
  }
  th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
  for (n in nodes) {
    if (n$type %in% c("latent", "data")) {
      s <- if (is.null(n$w)) 1 else n$w / r
      polygon(n$x + s * r * cos(th), n$y + r * sin(th), lwd = 1.5,
              col = if (n$type == "data") "grey75" else "white")
    } else {
      h <- half(n)
      rect(n$x - h[1], n$y - h[2], n$x + h[1], n$y + h[2], lwd = 1.2, lty = n$lty,
           col = if (n$type == "covariate") "grey75" else "white")
    }
    text(n$x, n$y, n$lab, cex = cex)
  }
}

nd <- function(id, lab, x, y, type = "latent", w = NULL, lty = 1) {
  list(id = id, lab = lab, x = x, y = y, type = type, w = w, lty = lty)
}

levels_rs <- data.frame(lab = c("Level 1: year t", "Level 2: stand j",
                                "Level 3: population", "Fixed: prior settings"),
                        ymin = c(0, 2.4, 4.6, 6.4), ymax = c(2.4, 4.6, 6.4, 7.8))
plates_rs <- function(x0, x1) list(
  list(x0 = x0, x1 = x1, y0 = 0.08, y1 = 4.3, lab = "stands j = 1, ..., 12", left = TRUE),
  list(x0 = x0 + 0.2, x1 = x1 - 0.2, y0 = 0.42, y1 = 1.95, lab = "years t"))
```

# Bayesian hierarchical models {#bayesian-hierarchical}

Last week we fit mixed models by maximum likelihood; this week we go
Bayesian! This part defines what makes a model 'hierarchical', works
through partial pooling (a major advantage of hierarchical models), and
then fits the drought random slope model by MCMC using `brms` (with a bonus section in Stan).

## 1. What makes a model hierarchical? {#what-hierarchical}

A **hierarchical model** is composed of two or more layers. The data are described
conditional on some unobserved quantities, and those quantities are in
turn drawn from a probability distribution whose parameters (often
called *hyperparameters*) are also estimated from the data.

For the drought data used below (the
[random slope](Week12_MixedModels.html#random-slopes) example):

- **data layer:** each ring width is Normal around its own stand's regression line,
  $\text{width}_{jt} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_a + a_j + (\mu_b + b_j)\,x_{jt},\ \sigma_e^2)$;
- **group layer:** the stand deviations come from one shared
  distribution, $(a_j, b_j) \sim \text{MVN}(0, G)$;
- **parameters:** $\mu_a$, $\mu_b$, $G$, and $\sigma_e$ are estimated (and
  in a Bayesian model, each gets a prior).

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) shows these layers as levels, stacked
from the data up. This one uses the priors from the [brms fit](#brms):

```{r dag-random-slope, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
nodes <- list(nd("se", quote(sigma[e]), 2.2, 5.5), nd("ma", quote(mu[a]), 3.6, 5.5),
              nd("mb", quote(mu[b]), 4.8, 5.5), nd("sa", quote(sigma[a]), 6.3, 5.5),
              nd("sb", quote(sigma[b]), 7.5, 5.5), nd("rho", quote(rho[ab]), 8.7, 5.5),
              nd("pse", "half-N(0, 0.3)", 2.2, 7.0, "fixed"),
              nd("pma", "N(1, 0.5)", 3.85, 7.0, "fixed"), nd("pmb", "N(0, 0.5)", 5.15, 7.0, "fixed"),
              nd("ps", "half-N(0, 0.3)", 6.9, 7.0, "fixed"), nd("plkj", "LKJ(2)", 8.7, 7.0, "fixed"),
              nd("ab", quote(list(a[j], b[j])), 7.2, 3.3, w = 0.62),
              nd("y", quote(width[jt]), 5.2, 1.25, "data", w = 0.62),
              nd("x", quote(x[jt]), 7.2, 1.25, "covariate"))
edges <- rbind(c("pma", "ma"), c("pmb", "mb"), c("ps", "sa"), c("ps", "sb"), c("plkj", "rho"),
               c("pse", "se"), c("sa", "ab"), c("sb", "ab"), c("rho", "ab"),
               c("ma", "y"), c("mb", "y"), c("ab", "y"), c("x", "y"), c("se", "y"))
draw_level_dag(nodes, edges, levels_rs, plates_rs(4.0, 8.4), xlim = c(0, 9.6))
```

Each arrow points from a quantity to one whose distribution is written
in terms of it. Open circles are unknowns the model estimates, the
shaded oval is the data, the shaded square is a measured covariate
(precipitation), and white boxes are prior settings we choose. A
rectangle (a *plate*) means "repeat what's inside": once per stand,
and within each stand once per year.^[These DAGs are a different use
of the idea than the [causal diagrams](Week10_ModelComparison.html#dags)
of Week 10. There an arrow claims that one real-world variable affects
another. Here an arrow describes the model: each node's distribution is
written conditional on its parents, and the joint distribution of
everything is the product of those conditional pieces. Diagrams like
this are also called Bayesian networks or plate diagrams.]

Read from the bottom up. Each ring width (level 1) depends on its
stand's deviations $(a_j, b_j)$ (level 2), and every stand's deviations
depend on the same $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_b$, and $\rho_{ab}$ (level 3).
That shared level is what makes the model hierarchical. The mean
intercept and slope and the residual SD are shared too, but they act on
the data directly, so their arrows skip level 2.

Categories/groups are only one kind of unobserved layer. In a spatial model it is
a surface over the landscape, with nearby sites more alike than distant
ones (a Gaussian process like the one in [Gaussian processes](#gp), with
distance in place of temperature). In capture-recapture and occupancy
models it is each animal's or site's true state (alive or dead,
occupied or not), with one process describing how the state changes
(survival) and another describing what we see given the state
(detection). What these models share is a model for the data given
something we never observe directly, plus a model for that unobserved
thing.

Every model with random effects is hierarchical; "mixed model" and
"multilevel model" are other names for this kind. The reverse doesn't
hold: the occupancy and state-space models above are hierarchical, but
nobody calls them 'mixed models'. 

The stand intercepts and slopes in the 
data layer have the same function as a fixed intercept and slope, but they
are treated as random draws from a population of stands. This is in contrast
to the fixed effects, which are treated as
separate and independently estimated unknown constants.

One clarification: the above definition might make it seem like every 
Bayesian model should be hierarchical - after all, a prior is like a second 'layer'.
However, a prior doesn't by itself make a model hierarchical. Compare two
Bayesian models for the drought slopes (leaving the intercepts aside).
Both give each stand its own slope $b_j$ in the data layer; they differ
in where the prior on $b_j$ comes from.

- **One layer (stand as a fixed factor):**
  $b_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$ for each stand. We choose the prior's
  mean and SD before seeing the data. Each stand's slope is estimated
  completely separately, learning nothing from the data collected at the
  other stands. A Normal(0, 1) prior is so wide
  (slopes are about 0.25 mm per 10 cm) that S12's estimate is close to
  its own least-squares slope. The result: no 'pooling' of information!
- **Two layers (stand as a random effect):**
  $b_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_b, \sigma_b^2)$, where the mean slope $\mu_b$
  and the among-stand SD $\sigma_b$ are unknown and get priors of their
  own (hyperpriors), such as $\sigma_b \sim \text{half-Normal}(0, 0.3)$ in
  the [brms fit](#brms). Now all 12 stands together tell us how
  much slopes vary. If the stands with long records have similar slopes,
  $\sigma_b$ is small and S12's slope is pulled strongly toward $\mu_b$; if
  they differ a lot, $\sigma_b$ is large and S12 keeps more of its own
  slope. This is the idea of [partial pooling](#partial-pooling) of information.

The data layer is the same in both models. The difference is who sets
the prior's SD -- either we choose it (no partial pooling) or we let the data 
determine how strongly each stand is pulled toward the others (partial pooling).
As DAGs (intercepts left out, as above):

```{r dag-contrast, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.1}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
common <- list(nd("x", quote(x[jt]), 6.4, 1.2, "covariate"),
               nd("y", quote(width[jt]), 4.5, 1.2, "data", w = 0.7),
               nd("se", quote(sigma[e]), 9.1, 5.5),
               nd("pse", "half-N(0, 0.3)", 9.1, 7.0, "fixed"))
common_edges <- rbind(c("x", "y"), c("se", "y"), c("pse", "se"), c("b", "y"))
draw_level_dag(c(common, list(nd("b", quote(b[j]), 4.5, 3.3),
                              nd("pb", "Normal(0, 1)", 4.5, 7.0, "fixed"))),
               rbind(common_edges, c("pb", "b")),
               levels_rs, plates_rs(3.3, 7.5), xlim = c(0, 10.3),
               main = "One layer: stand as a fixed factor")
draw_level_dag(c(common, list(nd("b", quote(b[j]), 4.5, 3.3),
                              nd("mb", quote(mu[b]), 3.7, 5.5),
                              nd("sb", quote(sigma[b]), 5.6, 5.5),
                              nd("pmb", "N(0, 0.5)", 3.1, 7.0, "fixed"),
                              nd("psb", "half-N(0, 0.3)", 6.0, 7.0, "fixed"))),
               rbind(common_edges, c("mb", "b"), c("sb", "b"), c("pmb", "mb"), c("psb", "sb")),
               levels_rs, plates_rs(3.3, 7.5), xlim = c(0, 10.3),
               main = "Two layers: stand as a random effect")
```

On the left, the arrow into $b_j$ comes straight from a box of numbers
we chose. Nothing estimated sits above the slopes, so one stand's data
can't change another stand's slope. On the right, every $b_j$ has the
same two estimated parents, $\mu_b$ and $\sigma_b$. Each stand's data
inform $\mu_b$ and $\sigma_b$, and those in turn inform every other
stand's slope. Both models share $\sigma_e$ across stands, but a shared
residual SD doesn't pool the slopes.

One misconception that I had for a long time is that a 'hierarchical model'
necessarily has more than one probability distribution contributing to the 
likelihood. This isn't actually true: integrating out a layer can
collapse the hierarchy into a single distribution (often but not always a multivariate Normal). 
For example, a Normal random intercept plus Normal noise gives a single 
multivariate Normal for all the observations (the
[block-diagonal $V$](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#random-intercept)). 
Similarly, a Poisson count whose rate varies according to a gamma distribution
gives the [negative binomial](Week4_ProbabilityDistributions.html#compounding).
In both cases the model can be written in a layered (*conditional*)
form, with the unobserved stand effects or rates, or in a collapsed
(*marginal*) form, with those integrated out. For the same data the
two give the same likelihood and the same estimates of the shared
parameters.

So is the marginal form hierarchical? If it came from integrating out a
layer, it is still hierarchical since it is the same model, written a different way. 
^[One nuance is that if the likelihood is specified directly as a
multivariate Normal with pre-specified correlations in the variance-covariance
matrix (e.g., correlation within stands in the random intercept framework),
and fitted directly using a function like `gls()`, there
is no easy way to recover information about the specific random slopes or intercepts
in the data-layer model. Therefore, these models are often NOT called 'hierarchical'
(instead, these models are usually called marginal or
correlated-errors models). For example, a negative binomial likelihood is simply
a convenient distribution for overdispersed counts. Even though
we COULD specify the NB likelihood as a Poisson count with an
unobserved, gamma-distributed rate (a hierarchical model) we typically don't call this
a hierarchical model.]
`lmer()` maximizes the marginal likelihood, and we still call a random
intercept model fit with `lmer()` 'hierarchical'. The
hierarchical structure is just folded into $V$: the within-stand
correlation is $\sigma_a^2 / (\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_e^2)$, and $\sigma_a$
is still the SD of the stand effects.^[Capture-recapture analysis (which I work with a lot!) works the same way: we usually
integrate the likelihood across all possible alive/dead states an animal could
have had, resulting in a single likelihood function (often a multinomial distribution).]

In practice the layered form is usually worth writing down anyway:
it says where the extra variation and correlation come from (e.g., differences among 
stands), and it is the only form that gives an estimate for each
stand (resulting in shrinkage/partial-pooling).


## 2. Partial pooling by hand {#pooling-by-hand}

```{r pooling-numbers, echo=FALSE}
pool_mu <- 3
pool_sb <- 0.5
pool_s <- 1
pool_n <- c(A = 4, B = 16)
pool_ybar <- c(A = 4.2, B = 4.0)
pool_w <- pool_sb^2 / (pool_sb^2 + pool_s^2 / pool_n)
pool_est <- pool_mu + pool_w * (pool_ybar - pool_mu)
```

Before fitting anything, here is what partial pooling does to a single
group. A random intercept model estimates each group's mean by pulling
its own sample mean toward the overall mean. For group $j$, with $n_j$
observations and sample mean $\bar y_j$, the estimated group mean
($\theta_j = \mu + a_j$) is

$$\hat\theta_j = \hat\mu + w_j(\bar y_j - \hat\mu), \qquad
w_j = \frac{\sigma_a^2}{\sigma_a^2 + \sigma_e^2/n_j},$$

where $\hat\mu$ is the overall mean, $\sigma_a$ the SD among groups,
and $\sigma_e$ the SD within a group. The weight $w_j$ compares the
spread among groups with the sampling variance of the group's own mean
(see the [bonus derivation](#pooling-formula)).
Here it is applied to the *Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis* (Bd)
infection load in two ponds. Across many ponds the mean load is
$\hat\mu =$ `r pool_mu` (log$_{10}$ zoospore equivalents per swab), ponds
differ with SD $\sigma_a =$ `r pool_sb`, and frogs within a pond differ
with SD $\sigma_e =$ `r pool_s`. Pond A had `r pool_n["A"]` frogs swabbed
with mean load `r pool_ybar["A"]`; pond B had `r pool_n["B"]` frogs with
mean `r pool_ybar["B"]`.

- Pond A: $\sigma_e^2/n = `r 1 / pool_n["A"]`$, so
  $w_A = `r pool_sb^2` / (`r pool_sb^2` + `r 1 / pool_n["A"]`) = `r pool_w["A"]`$
  and $\hat\theta_A = `r pool_mu` + `r pool_w["A"]` \times `r pool_ybar["A"] - pool_mu` = `r pool_est["A"]`$.
- Pond B: $\sigma_e^2/n = `r 1 / pool_n["B"]`$, so
  $w_B = `r pool_sb^2` / (`r pool_sb^2` + `r 1 / pool_n["B"]`) = `r pool_w["B"]`$
  and $\hat\theta_B = `r pool_mu` + `r pool_w["B"]` \times `r pool_ybar["B"] - pool_mu` = `r pool_est["B"]`$.

```{r pooling-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.4}
par(mar = c(4, 7.5, 0.5, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(2.8, 4.4), ylim = c(0.5, 2.5), yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
     xlab = expression(log[10] ~ "zoospore equivalents"))
axis(2, at = 1:2, labels = c("pond B (16)", "pond A (4)"), las = 1)
abline(v = pool_mu, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
arrows(pool_ybar[c("B", "A")], 1:2, pool_est[c("B", "A")], 1:2, length = 0.08, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
points(pool_ybar[c("B", "A")], 1:2, pch = 1, cex = 1.4)
points(pool_est[c("B", "A")], 1:2, pch = 19, col = "steelblue", cex = 1.4)
text(pool_mu, 2.45, "overall mean", pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = "grey40")
```

Pond A has the higher raw mean, but after pooling pond B has the higher
estimate! Four frogs give a noisy pond mean (sampling variance
`r 1 / pool_n["A"]`, as large as the among-pond variance
`r pool_sb^2`), so half of pond A's distance from the overall mean is
treated as noise. With a much larger sample size (n = 16) pond B gets to keep 
most of its own mean (it 'earned' this via its large sample size!).

As $n_j$ grows, $w_j \to 1$ and the group
keeps its own mean (no pooling). As $\sigma_a \to 0$, $w_j \to 0$ and
every group gets the overall mean (complete pooling).

Pulling each group's estimate toward the overall mean like this is
called **shrinkage**: the distance $\bar y_j - \mu$ shrinks by the
factor $w_j$. Groups with low sample size shrink the most. Each group
borrows information from the full set of observations: global
information used for local inference.
Extreme group means are partly luck, so
shrinking them makes the estimates less variable -- and generally more accurate 
when averaged over groups -- at the cost of a little bias toward the global mean.
This is actually the same idea as the
[ridge and lasso penalties](Week10_ModelComparison.html#regularization),
which also 'shrink' coefficients toward zero. The difference is where the
shrinkage comes from: ridge regression chooses its penalty
$\lambda$ (often by a separate cross-validation step), while a random intercept model
estimates $\sigma_a$ from the data at the same time as the other parameters are 
estimated (and $\sigma_a$ sets every $w_j$: see the [ridge bonus](#ridge-prior)).

## 3. Partial pooling {#partial-pooling}

To see partial pooling across many groups, let's go back to the simulated
drought-sensitivity data from
[random slopes](Week12_MixedModels.html#random-slopes): ring widths at
12 pinyon stands whose records run from 5 to 30 years. Precipitation is
in 10-cm units centered at 20 cm, so a stand's intercept is its ring
width in a 20-cm winter and its slope is the change in width per extra
10 cm precipitation.

```{r drought-data}
library(mvtnorm)
library(lme4)
set.seed(12)
n_years <- rep(c(30, 24, 18, 12, 8, 5), each = 2)        # record length per stand
sd_true <- c(0.15, 0.10)                                   # among-stand SDs: intercept, slope
rho_true <- -0.6
G_true <- diag(sd_true) %*% matrix(c(1, rho_true, rho_true, 1), 2) %*% diag(sd_true)
ab_true <- rmvnorm(12, c(0.9, 0.25), G_true)              # each stand's intercept and slope
stand_names <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:12)
drought <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, n_years)),
                      year = unlist(lapply(n_years, function(n) seq(2021 - n, 2020))))
j <- as.integer(drought$stand)
drought$precip <- round(rgamma(nrow(drought), shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1)
drought$precip10 <- (drought$precip - 20) / 10
drought$width <- round(ab_true[j, 1] + ab_true[j, 2] * drought$precip10 +
                         rnorm(nrow(drought), 0, 0.12), 2)

# no pooling: one least-squares line per stand; and the maximum likelihood random slope fit
nopool <- t(sapply(split(drought, drought$stand), function(s) coef(lm(width ~ precip10, data = s))))
fit_rs_lmer <- lmer(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
ml <- c(fixef(fit_rs_lmer), as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_rs_lmer))$sdcor)
names(ml) <- c("mu_a", "mu_b", "sigma_a", "sigma_b", "rho_ab", "sigma_e")
round(ml, 3)
```

```{r drought-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(width ~ precip, data = drought, col = "grey60", pch = 16, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Winter precipitation (cm)", ylab = "Ring width (mm)")
for (s in seq_len(12)) {
  xr <- range(drought$precip10[drought$stand == stand_names[s]])
  lines(20 + 10 * xr, nopool[s, 1] + nopool[s, 2] * xr, lwd = ifelse(n_years[s] <= 8, 1, 2),
        lty = ifelse(n_years[s] <= 8, 2, 1))
}
legend("topleft", c("stand with 12-30 years", "stand with 5-8 years"), lty = 1:2, lwd = 2:1,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
plot(nopool, pch = 19, xlab = "Intercept: width at 20 cm (mm)",
     ylab = "Slope (mm per 10 cm)", cex = 1.1, xlim = range(nopool[, 1]) + c(0, 0.05))
text(nopool, labels = stand_names, pos = 4, cex = 0.7, col = "grey40")
```

Left: one least-squares line per stand. Right: each stand's own
intercept and slope (the "no pooling" estimates).

There are three ways to estimate each stand's mean ring width:

- **complete pooling:** ignore stands; every stand gets the overall mean;
- **no pooling:** estimate each stand separately (stand as a fixed
  factor);
- **partial pooling:** the random effect, a compromise between the two!

With partial pooling, each stand's mean ring width gets a prior built from 
all the other stands: it's centered on the overall mean,
and its SD ($\sigma_a$) reflects how much stands differ from one
another. The random slope model does the same thing for each stand's
slope.

Ignoring precipitation for the moment, here is the random intercept
fit, checked against the formula:

```{r pooling-check}
fit_ri0 <- lmer(width ~ 1 + (1 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
sd_ri0 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_ri0))$sdcor          # sigma_a, sigma_e
ybar <- tapply(drought$width, drought$stand, mean)
n_j <- as.vector(table(drought$stand))
w <- sd_ri0[1]^2 / (sd_ri0[1]^2 + sd_ri0[2]^2 / n_j)
round(cbind(own_mean = ybar, n_j, w, formula = fixef(fit_ri0) + w * (ybar - fixef(fit_ri0)),
            lmer = coef(fit_ri0)$stand[, 1]), 3)
```

The formula matches `lmer()`'s stand estimates. Here
$\hat\sigma_a =$ `r f3(sd_ri0[1])` and $\hat\sigma_e =$ `r f3(sd_ri0[2])`;
the widget starts at those values. It plots each stand's own mean and
its partially pooled estimate.

```{r widget-pooling, echo=FALSE}
widget("partial_pooling.html")
```

> **Question:** Set $\sigma_a$ to 0, then drag it to 0.4. Which two
> pooling choices are these? Then compare S10 and S12: their means
> are similar (`r f2(ybar["S10"])` and `r f2(ybar["S12"])`), but one has
> 8 years and the other 5. Which moves more toward the overall mean, and
> why?

## 4. Fitting hierarchical models by MCMC {#re-priors}

The random slope model (the layers at the
[top of this part](#bayesian-hierarchical)) pools intercepts and slopes
together. The stand deviations share one distribution,
$(a_j, b_j) \sim \text{MVN}(0, G)$, with

$$G = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_a^2 & \rho_{ab}\,\sigma_a\sigma_b \\ \rho_{ab}\,\sigma_a\sigma_b & \sigma_b^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

where $\sigma_a$ and $\sigma_b$ are the among-stand SDs of the intercepts
and slopes and $\rho_{ab}$ is their correlation. The `lmer()` fit in
[partial pooling](#partial-pooling) estimated these by maximum
likelihood (`ml`), integrating the stand effects out of the likelihood.

As discussed above, a Bayesian fit usually keeps the stand effects in the
model explicitly. We put priors on
the population-level parameters ($\mu_a$, $\mu_b$, $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_b$,
$\rho_{ab}$, $\sigma_e$), and the sampler draws each stand's random intercept and
slope along with everything else (every open circle in the
[DAG](#what-hierarchical)). In Bayesian/MCMC fitting, the hierarchical nature
of these models is fully front and center (in a way, Bayesian models are more 'hierarchical'
than frequentist versions of the same model because the hierarchy is made explicit!).
That is why 'Bayesian' and 'hierarchical' are nearly synonymous in some circles!
This also makes hierarchical models much easier to fit from scratch (both conceptually and practically), 
which is one reason Bayesian methods are so widely used
in ecology and environmental science. Compared with maximum likelihood:

- **No integral.** The sampler draws the $a_j$ and $b_j$ instead of
  integrating them out, so a Poisson or binomial response is no harder
  than a Normal one.^[Marginalizing a Normal model only takes building
  the covariance matrix of a multivariate Normal, which is much more
  straightforward than integrating across the random effects for other
  response distributions.]
- **Uncertainty carries through.** Each stand's estimate reflects
  uncertainty in $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_b$, and $\rho_{ab}$, rather than plugging in
  their best values.
- **Priors help with few groups.** A weakly informative prior keeps an
  SD off the boundary at 0 and a correlation off $\pm 1$, where
  maximum likelihood 'gave up' with four stands (see
  [Q3 here](Week12_MixedModels.html#variance-discussion)).
- **The price** (as with all Bayesian models) is choosing priors and checking the sampler (see
  [checking chains](Week9_MCMC.html#chain-checks)).

## 5. Priors for a covariance matrix {#lkj}

The random slope model needs a prior on $G$, a 2 $\times$ 2 covariance
matrix. The usual approach splits $G$ into scales and correlations,

$$G = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_a & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_b \end{pmatrix}
\Omega
\begin{pmatrix} \sigma_a & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_b \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Omega = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho_{ab} \\ \rho_{ab} & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

and puts separate priors on each piece: a half-Normal, half-$t$, or
exponential prior on each SD, and an **LKJ prior** on the
correlation matrix $\Omega$.^[The LKJ prior is named for Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe (2009, *Journal of
Multivariate Analysis*).
Older BUGS and JAGS code often used an inverse-Wishart prior on $G$
instead, which ties the prior on the SDs to the prior on the
correlations; splitting them makes each easier to choose.]

The LKJ density has one shape parameter $\eta$:

$$p(\Omega) \propto \det(\Omega)^{\eta - 1}$$

For a 2 $\times$ 2 matrix, $\det(\Omega) = 1 - \rho_{ab}^2$, so
$p(\rho_{ab}) \propto (1 - \rho_{ab}^2)^{\eta - 1}$. With $\eta = 1$ every
correlation is equally likely; $\eta > 1$ favors correlations near 0,
and $\eta < 1$ favors correlations near $\pm 1$. For a bigger matrix
($K \times K$), each single correlation has the marginal prior
$(\rho + 1)/2 \sim \text{Beta}(\eta - 1 + K/2,\ \eta - 1 + K/2)$.

```{r widget-lkj, echo=FALSE}
widget("lkj_prior.html")
```

> **Question:** For a 10 $\times$ 10 correlation matrix with $\eta = 1$,
> how likely is any one correlation to exceed 0.5 in absolute value?
> What does "uniform" mean for a matrix that large?

## 6. The random slope model in brms {#brms}

`brms` writes and runs the Stan program for a model given as an
`lme4`-style formula. Priors go in the `prior` argument, one
`prior()` call per group of parameters, combined with `c()`. Each call
names a distribution in Stan's syntax and a `class`: `b` for
fixed-effect slopes, `Intercept`, `sd` for the among-group SDs, `cor`
for their correlations, and `sigma` for the residual SD. A `coef` or
`group` argument narrows a prior to one parameter or one grouping
factor. `brms` already bounds SDs at zero, so `normal(0, 0.3)` on class
`sd` is a half-Normal. `get_prior(formula, data)` lists every
parameter that can take a prior, with its default. The
[brms and rstanarm handout](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_BayesianMixedModelSyntax.pdf)
has the syntax for other random-effect structures, residual
correlation, and non-Normal responses.

The order of the `prior()` calls does not matter. `brms` matches each
one to parameters by its `class`, `coef`, and `group`, not by its
position. When two priors could apply to the same parameter, the more
specific one wins wherever it sits in the list: a prior with
`coef = "precip10"` overrides a class-wide `b` prior. Giving the same
parameter two priors at the same level is an error.

Here is the random slope model with Normal priors on the mean
intercept and slope, half-Normal(0, 0.3) priors on the among-stand SDs
and on $\sigma_e$, and an LKJ(2) prior on the correlation. Mean ring width
is around 1 mm, so Normal(1, 0.5) on the intercept rules out
implausible values (a mean width of 3 mm, or a negative one) but is
otherwise vague; Normal(0, 0.5) on the slope allows a change of up to
about 1 mm per 10 cm of precipitation in either direction.^[`brms` puts the `Intercept` prior on the
intercept at the *sample mean* of each predictor, not at zero. Here the
mean of `precip10` is `r round(mean(drought$precip10), 2)`, so the two
are close.]

```{r brms-fit, cache=TRUE, results="hide"}
library(brms)
fit_brms <- brm(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought,
                prior = c(prior(normal(1, 0.5), class = Intercept),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = sd),
                          prior(lkj(2), class = cor),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = sigma)),
                backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0)
```

Check the sampler first (no divergent transitions, $\hat R$ near 1,
large effective sample sizes; see
[checking chains](Week9_MCMC.html#chain-checks)), then the estimates:

```{r brms-summary}
summary(fit_brms)
```

`prior_summary(fit_brms)` lists every prior in a fit.^[Without the
`prior` argument, `brms` uses an LKJ(1) prior on the correlations and
half-Student-$t$ priors on the SDs. `rstanarm::stan_lmer()` fits the
same formula from precompiled models, so it skips the compile step.]

```{r brms-numbers, echo=FALSE}
library(posterior)
draws <- as_draws_df(fit_brms)
q <- function(v) quantile(v, c(0.5, 0.05, 0.95))
post <- rbind(mu_a = q(draws$b_Intercept), mu_b = q(draws$b_precip10),
              sigma_a = q(draws$sd_stand__Intercept), sigma_b = q(draws$sd_stand__precip10),
              rho_ab = q(draws$cor_stand__Intercept__precip10), sigma_e = q(draws$sigma))
ml_vs_bayes <- data.frame(truth = c(0.9, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, -0.6, 0.12),
                          lmer = ml, post)
names(ml_vs_bayes)[3:5] <- c("posterior median", "5%", "95%")
ab_post <- coef(fit_brms)$stand[, "Estimate", ]          # posterior means, one row per stand
err <- function(est, rows = 1:12) colMeans(abs(est[rows, ] - ab_true[rows, ]))
short_rows <- which(n_years <= 8)
err_nopool_short <- err(nopool, short_rows)
err_post_short <- err(ab_post, short_rows)
```

```{r ml-bayes-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(ml_vs_bayes, digits = 3, caption = "Maximum likelihood (lmer) and posterior summaries")
```

The two methods agree closely on everything except the correlation: the
MLE is `r f2(ml["rho_ab"])`, while the posterior median is
`r f2(post["rho_ab", 1])` with a 90% interval from `r f2(post["rho_ab", 2])`
to `r f2(post["rho_ab", 3])`.

```{r rho-posterior, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.6}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
hist(draws$cor_stand__Intercept__precip10, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white", xlim = c(-1, 1),
     main = "", xlab = expression(rho[ab] ~ "(intercept-slope correlation)"))
curve(dbeta((x + 1) / 2, 2, 2) / 2, add = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = ml["rho_ab"], lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
abline(v = -0.6, lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("topright", c("LKJ(2) prior", "MLE (lmer)", "truth"), lty = c(2, 1, 3), lwd = 2,
       col = c("black", "firebrick", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

```{r shrinkage-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(nopool, pch = 1, cex = 1.2, xlab = "Intercept: width at 20 cm (mm)",
     ylab = "Slope (mm per 10 cm)",
     xlim = range(nopool[, 1], ab_post[, 1]) + c(0, 0.06), ylim = range(nopool[, 2], ab_post[, 2]))
arrows(nopool[, 1], nopool[, 2], ab_post[, 1], ab_post[, 2], length = 0.07, col = "steelblue")
points(ab_post, pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
text(nopool, labels = paste0(stand_names, " (", n_years, ")"), pos = 4, cex = 0.65, col = "grey40")
points(post["mu_a", 1], post["mu_b", 1], pch = 3, cex = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("own least-squares fit", "posterior mean", "population mean"),
       pch = c(1, 19, 3), col = c("black", "steelblue", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

Each arrow runs from a stand's own fit to its posterior mean; the
number in parentheses is the record length. Stands with short records
move the most; stands with 24 or 30 years barely move.

```{r shrink-sims, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(746)
shrink_sims <- t(replicate(500, {
  ab <- rmvnorm(12, c(0.9, 0.25), G_true)
  sim <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, n_years)))
  k <- as.integer(sim$stand)
  sim$x <- (round(rgamma(nrow(sim), shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1) - 20) / 10
  sim$y <- ab[k, 1] + ab[k, 2] * sim$x + rnorm(nrow(sim), 0, 0.12)
  np <- t(sapply(split(sim, sim$stand), function(s) coef(lm(y ~ x, data = s))))
  pp <- as.matrix(coef(lmer(y ~ x + (x | stand), data = sim, REML = FALSE))$stand)
  sh <- n_years <= 8
  c(np_a = mean(abs(np - ab)[sh, 1]), np_b = mean(abs(np - ab)[sh, 2]),
    pp_a = mean(abs(pp - ab)[sh, 1]), pp_b = mean(abs(pp - ab)[sh, 2]))
}))
```

Because the data are simulated, we can compare both sets of estimates
with the true stand values. For the four stands with 5 or 8 years, the
average error in the slopes is `r f3(err_nopool_short[2])` mm per 10 cm
with no pooling and `r f3(err_post_short[2])` with partial pooling
(intercepts: `r f3(err_nopool_short[1])` and `r f3(err_post_short[1])`
mm). That's a mixed result: in any one data set, shrinkage can pull a
stand that really is unusual too far toward the mean. The advantage is
that we will do better on average! Over `r nrow(shrink_sims)` simulated data sets with the same
design, using `lmer()`'s stand estimates, partial pooling cut the
average slope error for the short-record stands from
`r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "np_b"]))` to `r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "pp_b"]))`
(intercepts: `r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "np_a"]))` to
`r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "pp_a"]))`).

> **Question:** Why is the posterior for $\rho_{ab}$ so much wider than the
> other posteriors, and why is its median closer to 0 than the MLE?
> Which summary is more honest about what 12 stands can tell us?

> **Question:** Change `lkj(2)` to `lkj(1)`, then to `lkj(10)`, and
> refit. Predict how the posterior for $\rho_{ab}$ will move before you run
> each one. Do the stand estimates change much?
